cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Require large grocery stores to donate safe, unsold food to local hunger-relief organizations.
2. Create a citywide app that connects businesses with charities able to collect surplus food.
3. Offer grants for food banks to purchase refrigerated vehicles and cold-storage equipment.
4. Establish neighborhood community fridges with clear food-safety rules and regular maintenance.
5. Help restaurants offer discounted surplus meals through end-of-day sales platforms.
6. Encourage supermarkets to mark down products approaching their sell-by dates.
7. Run public workshops explaining the difference between food quality dates and safety guidance.
8. Teach residents how to plan meals around ingredients they already have.
9. Distribute refrigerator storage guides that help households keep produce fresh longer.
10. Offer community classes on freezing, pickling, drying, and other food-preservation methods.
11. Help schools adjust meal purchasing using attendance data and student demand.
12. Introduce school share tables where students can leave eligible unopened food for others.
13. Give students enough seated lunch time to finish their meals.
14. Let students choose age-appropriate portion sizes rather than serving identical portions.
15. Train cafeteria staff to prepare food in smaller batches as demand becomes clear.
16. Organize volunteer gleaning teams to collect edible crops left in nearby farm fields.
17. Coordinate volunteers to harvest surplus fruit from residential trees with owners’ permission.
18. Support retailers that sell cosmetically imperfect produce at reduced prices.
19. Create a neighborhood exchange platform for surplus garden vegetables and herbs.
20. Help farmers’ markets arrange end-of-market food pickups by local charities.
21. Require city-funded events to submit plans for preventing and redistributing food waste.
22. Promote smaller default portions at restaurants while allowing customers to request more.
23. Encourage restaurants to offer side dishes as optional add-ons rather than automatic servings.
24. Make take-home containers readily available for restaurant leftovers.
25. Help restaurants simplify menus so ingredients can be used across multiple dishes.
26. Provide small businesses with affordable inventory-management software that flags aging stock.
27. Train food-service workers to use first-in, first-out storage systems.
28. Fund food-waste audits for hospitals, universities, hotels, and other large institutions.
29. Encourage caterers to use confirmed headcounts and reservation updates when planning quantities.
30. Replace oversized buffet displays with smaller trays replenished as needed.
31. Create a shared commercial kitchen where businesses can turn surplus ingredients into saleable products.
32. Support businesses that transform surplus bread, fruit, or vegetables into new food products.
33. Offer microgrants for neighborhood organizations to host meals using rescued ingredients.
34. Establish a rapid-response network to recover refrigerated food during power outages.
35. Provide backup-power grants for food banks and other critical food-storage facilities.
36. Create multilingual guidance on safely cooling, storing, and reheating leftovers.
37. Lend food dehydrators, canning equipment, and vacuum sealers through public libraries.
38. Encourage apartment buildings to provide shared freezer space for residents.
39. Help employers arrange safe redistribution of untouched meeting and cafeteria food.
40. Encourage grocery stores to sell loose produce so shoppers can buy only what they need.
41. Support smaller package sizes for perishable staples commonly purchased by one-person households.
42. Work with retailers to replace waste-promoting multibuy offers with equivalent single-item discounts.
43. Publish a directory of food-donation locations, accepted items, and collection hours.
44. Offer food donors training on applicable liability protections and safe donation practices.
45. Recognize businesses that achieve independently verified reductions in edible food waste.
46. Measure citywide food-waste generation regularly and publish progress toward reduction targets.
47. Provide curbside compost collection for unavoidable household food scraps.
48. Establish neighborhood composting hubs where curbside collection is unavailable.
49. Route suitable food scraps to permitted animal-feed operations when safe and lawful.
50. Send unavoidable food waste that cannot be otherwise recovered to anaerobic digestion facilities that capture energy and manage digestate safely.

cells.state_text: A bruised pear at a closing market; a kitchen window lighting up across town. They touch in the hour between unwanted and needed, and perhaps some of a city’s food waste is really a mismatch of clocks, not a shortage of appetite.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide alert service that connects closing-time market vendors with nearby residents willing to buy discounted surplus.
2. Encourage supermarkets to mark down perishables progressively before they expire rather than discard them at full price.
3. Publish clear guidance explaining the difference between food quality dates and safety-related expiration dates.
4. Install monitored community refrigerators in accessible locations where residents can safely share surplus food.
5. Organize volunteer gleaning teams to collect crops left behind on farms surrounding the city.
6. Create a purchasing program that connects cosmetically imperfect local produce with schools, hospitals, and municipal kitchens.
7. Help small food businesses forecast demand using shared tools that account for weather, holidays, and local events.
8. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portions at proportionately lower prices.
9. Let restaurant customers decline or substitute sides they are unlikely to eat.
10. Make takeaway containers routinely available so diners can bring unfinished meals home.
11. Fund kitchen waste audits that show restaurants which ingredients and dishes are most frequently discarded.
12. Introduce school meal preordering so cafeterias can prepare closer to the number of meals students actually want.
13. Schedule elementary school recess before lunch to give children a better chance of arriving hungry and eating their meals.
14. Establish supervised school share tables for unopened foods that meet local safety requirements.
15. Replace mandatory cafeteria trays with optional trays to discourage taking more food than diners can finish.
16. Offer hospital patients meals on demand where feasible instead of delivering fixed meals regardless of appetite or treatment schedules.
17. Ask caterers to prepare large bookings in stages, keeping a safely stored reserve rather than putting every portion out immediately.
18. Require city-permitted festivals to arrange safe surplus-food collection before the event begins.
19. Build a shared cold-storage hub where small charities can hold donated perishables until distribution.
20. Operate a refrigerated rescue van on predictable routes between food businesses and community meal providers.
21. Recruit bicycle couriers to move small surplus donations quickly between nearby businesses and recipient organizations.
22. Provide donors with practical training on food safety, recordkeeping, and applicable donation protections.
23. Create standard donation agreements so businesses and charities do not have to negotiate every partnership from scratch.
24. Offer mini-grants for the insulated containers, freezers, and shelving needed to accept more rescued food.
25. Extend food pantry collection hours into evenings and weekends so donations reach people whose schedules exclude daytime visits.
26. Provide culturally appropriate cooking guides for unfamiliar ingredients commonly distributed through food assistance programs.
27. Offer a free meal-planning tool that builds shopping lists around ingredients residents already have.
28. Distribute refrigerator thermometers with guidance on safe temperatures to prevent premature spoilage at home.
29. Run neighborhood workshops on storing produce correctly, including which fruits and vegetables should be kept apart.
30. Publish flexible recipes that turn small amounts of leftover rice, vegetables, bread, and other foods into complete meals.
31. Encourage retailers to price smaller packages fairly so single-person households are not pushed into buying excess food.
32. Expand refill and bulk-buying options that let shoppers purchase only the quantities they need.
33. Partner with licensed processors to freeze seasonal produce surpluses for use in community meals throughout the year.
34. Open community kitchens for supervised preservation sessions that turn excess produce into safely canned, dried, or pickled foods.
35. Support businesses that transform food-processing byproducts, such as spent grain or fruit pulp, into edible products.
36. Encourage restaurants to offer a daily surplus-special dish built around safe ingredients that need using soon.
37. Train commercial cooks in root-to-stem techniques that use edible leaves, stalks, peels, and other commonly discarded parts.
38. Set up neighborhood produce swaps where gardeners can exchange harvests they cannot use.
39. Create a fruit-tree registry that allows owners to invite volunteers to harvest otherwise unpicked fruit.
40. Coordinate community garden planting schedules to reduce simultaneous gluts of the same crops.
41. Offer business grants tied to measured reductions in edible food waste rather than simply increased diversion from landfill.
42. Publish an annual city food-waste dashboard identifying major sources, seasonal patterns, and progress toward reduction targets.
43. Establish a voluntary business pledge with sector-specific reduction goals and public recognition for verified improvements.
44. Help grocery stores sell loose produce alongside packaged options so shoppers can buy individual items instead of oversized bundles.
45. Form neighborhood buying clubs that divide large wholesale orders into quantities individual households can realistically consume.
46. Install temperature alarms in shared food-storage facilities so staff can act before refrigeration failures spoil entire inventories.
47. Develop an emergency food-rescue plan for power outages, transport disruptions, and sudden business closures.
48. Create a business-to-business exchange where manufacturers and wholesalers can sell surplus ingredients in commercial quantities.
49. Require municipal departments to check existing food stocks before placing orders for meetings and public events.
50. Recruit trusted neighborhood ambassadors to normalize eating leftovers, freezing spare portions, and sharing food before it spoils.

12. A fortune teller gives a skeptical customer a refund after recognizing the customer from a recurring nightmare.

14. A nervous executioner asks the condemned prisoner to help assemble a flat-pack electric chair.

16. Two burglars hiding in a pantry discover they have independently broken into their own childhood home.

22. Two estranged friends record competing versions of the same childhood memory into an old cassette recorder.
23. A hostage negotiates with an amateur kidnapper to improve the lighting for their ransom video.
24. A newly elected president of a tiny club discovers the outgoing president has been its only other member for years.

26. A person preparing to propose drops the ring into a locked donation box and must convince their partner to help retrieve it without explaining why.
27. A therapist and client switch chairs as an exercise, and the client proves alarmingly good at the therapist’s job.
28. Two friends open a time capsule and find a photograph of themselves opening it.
29. A hotel guest asks a housekeeper to confirm that the room has become slightly smaller since yesterday.
30. Two siblings try to recreate their father’s signature laugh before either forgets how it sounded.
31. A security guard catches a thief stealing only the blank pages from a notebook.
32. A couple tests whether their smart speaker is listening by inventing a secret, then starts arguing about whether it sounds plausible.
33. A painter asks a portrait subject to stop smiling, but the subject insists they have not smiled once.
34. Two strangers attending a silent retreat discover they can have a vicious argument using only handwritten compliments.
35. A person teaching their partner a simple dance realizes every mistake is an attempt to delay their departure.
36. Two coworkers trapped in a supply closet discover that each believes the other arranged the situation as a romantic gesture.
37. A clock repairer and a customer watch a repaired clock count backward toward a moment neither wants to revisit.
38. Two roommates conduct a formal trial over a missing slice of cake, with one reluctantly serving as both defendant and judge.
39. A person arrives to buy a secondhand mirror and recognizes the seller as their reflection’s imaginary friend.
40. Two amateur spies exchange identical briefcases, then struggle to reverse the exchange without admitting they brought the wrong ones.
41. A hearing-aid technician realizes a customer has been pretending not to hear their partner’s apologies for years.
42. Two people preparing a surprise party gradually admit that neither knows the guest of honor well enough to choose a cake.
43. A hypnotist tries to wake a volunteer who claims the session finally made them feel rested.
44. Two exes meet to exchange keys and discover that neither has ever used the other’s key.
45. A game designer watches a tester solve a supposedly impossible puzzle by refusing to follow its rules.
46. Two sisters practice telling their parents that they are moving away, then discover they are planning to move to the same city.
47. A person assembling a crib with their partner admits they have no memory of agreeing to have a baby.
48. Two friends attempt to destroy an embarrassing photograph, but each keeps rescuing it for a different reason.
49. A monk teaching a visitor how to meditate becomes increasingly distracted by the visitor’s effortless serenity.
50. Two survivors waiting for an air-quality timer to reach zero debate whether the first thing they do outside should be practical or beautiful.
